name: FIM — Monitored System Executable/Driver Deleted
description: Detects deletion of a monitored executable, DLL or driver on a protected server. Deletion of system binaries can indicate defence tooling being removed, malware self-cleanup, or destructive activity.
note:
## Investigation
1. `file.path` is the removed binary; determine whether it was a security/monitoring component.
2. Correlate with process activity on the host.
## Response
If a security component was removed, isolate and investigate.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.dataset:"fim.event" and event.action:"deleted" and file.extension:("exe" or "dll" or "sys")

name: FIM — New Executable or DLL Created in a Windows System Directory
description: Detects a NEW executable, DLL or driver file appearing in a protected Windows system directory (System32/SysWOW64/drivers) on a monitored server. Legitimate binaries there change during patching (attributes_modified/updated); a brand-new binary is a strong indicator of malware drop, DLL side-loading, or a malicious driver.
note:
## Investigation
1. `file.path`/`file.name` is the new binary; `file.hash.sha256/sha1` — pivot to threat intel; `file.owner` and `host.name` give context.
2. Correlate with Windows 4688/PowerShell and Kaspersky on the same host/time.
## Response
If unknown/unsigned, quarantine the file and investigate the host for compromise.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.dataset:"fim.event" and event.action:"created" and file.extension:("exe" or "dll" or "sys") and file.path:(*System32* or *SysWOW64* or *\\drivers\\*)

name: Host — Mass File Change Burst (Possible Ransomware or Destruction)
description:
Attacker objective
Encrypt, overwrite or destroy files at scale — ransomware or a wiper rapidly writing, renaming and deleting many files on a host.

Attack logic
Ransomware and destructive malware touch a large number of files in a short window (encrypt-in-place, rename to a new extension, or delete). A host generating an unusually high volume of distinct file changes is exhibiting this pattern.

Why this detection works
Aggregating distinct changed files per host over the file-integrity stream distinguishes a mass-change burst from the routine handful of file changes a host makes during normal operation and patching.

False positives
A large software deployment, OS upgrade, or bulk migration/backup job on the host.

Tuning
Set the per-host file-count threshold above the routine change rate; allowlist scheduled deployment/patch windows and hosts; note that coverage is limited to FIM-monitored paths, so user-data encryption outside those paths may not be visible.

Required telemetry
File Integrity Monitoring (fim.event): event.action, file.path, file.extension, host.name.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. host.name is the affected host; review the volume of creates/renames/deletes and the file extensions.
2. A burst of renames to a common new extension, or mass deletion, indicates ransomware/wiper — isolate the host immediately.
3. Correlate with Kaspersky/Defender detections and the host's backup status; confirm against any planned deployment.
false_positives: A large software deployment, OS upgrade, or bulk migration/backup job on the host.
query:
FROM logs-fim.event-* METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE event.dataset == "fim.event" AND event.action IN ("created","updated","moved","deleted") AND host.name IS NOT NULL
| STATS files = COUNT_DISTINCT(file.path), creates = COUNT(CASE(event.action=="created",1,null)), renames = COUNT(CASE(event.action=="moved",1,null)), deletes = COUNT(CASE(event.action=="deleted",1,null)), extensions = VALUES(file.extension) BY host.name
| WHERE files >= 100

name: Windows — Kernel Driver (.sys) Created in a System Directory
description:
Attacker objective
Load malicious kernel code or a vulnerable driver (bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver) to gain kernel-level control, disable security tooling, or hide activity (rootkit).

Attack logic
Kernel drivers (.sys) placed in the system drivers directory can execute in kernel mode. Attackers drop a malicious or known-vulnerable driver there as a precursor to loading it. New driver files in this location are rare and high-risk.

Why this detection works
File-integrity monitoring records the creation of .sys files in the drivers directory, surfacing driver drops at the filesystem level even without process context.

False positives
Legitimate driver installation via Windows Update, an OEM/hardware driver package, or a software installer.

Tuning
Allowlist verified driver-deployment/patch processes; correlate with driver-load events and signature status; prioritise unsigned or unexpected driver names.

Required telemetry
File Integrity Monitoring (fim.event): file.path (drivers directory), file.extension, event.action, file.hash, host.name.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. file.name/file.hash identify the driver and host.name the system; check the hash reputation and signature.
2. Confirm whether the driver came from a legitimate update/installer; an unknown or unsigned driver is high-risk (BYOVD/rootkit).
3. Correlate the hash with Kaspersky/Defender and hunt for the driver being loaded.
false_positives: Legitimate driver installation via Windows Update, an OEM/hardware driver package, or a software installer.
query: event.dataset:"fim.event" and event.action:"created" and file.extension:("sys" or "SYS") and file.path:*drivers*

name: Windows — Scheduled Task Definition File Created or Modified
description:
Attacker objective
Persist or execute code on a schedule by creating or modifying a Windows scheduled task, whose definition is stored as a file under the system Tasks directory.

Attack logic
Windows stores each scheduled task as an XML definition file under the system Tasks folder. Creating or altering one of these files corresponds to creating or changing a scheduled task — a common persistence and execution technique.

Why this detection works
File-integrity monitoring records writes to the Tasks directory, surfacing scheduled-task changes at the filesystem level even where task-scheduler event logging is unavailable.

False positives
Legitimate software installation/update, Group Policy, or administration that creates scheduled tasks.

Tuning
Allowlist known software-deployment and management tooling; correlate with Windows scheduled-task events (4698) and the task's action/command where available; prioritise servers.

Required telemetry
File Integrity Monitoring (fim.event): file.path (system Tasks directory), event.action, host.name.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. file.path names the task definition and host.name the system.
2. Correlate with Windows event 4698 (scheduled task created) to identify the task action and the creating account (not captured by FIM).
3. Review the task's command/trigger; an unexpected task is persistence — remove and investigate.
false_positives: Legitimate software installation/update, Group Policy, or administration that creates scheduled tasks.
query: event.dataset:"fim.event" and event.action:("created" or "updated") and file.path:*\\System32\\Tasks\\*
